meta.intro: The vocabulary of the case file — forensics, investigation, and the courtroom, explained the way we use them on the show. Straight definitions, zero mystique.

terms.def: The foundation of forensic science: every contact between two objects leaves a trace. A perpetrator brings something to a scene and takes something away.
The documented, unbroken record of who handled a piece of evidence, when, and why. A gap can get the evidence excluded at trial.
Skin cells transferred by handling an object. Powerful but controversial — a few cells can travel on a handshake and land where their owner never was.
The FBI's Combined DNA Index System, linking DNA profiles across local, state, and national databases.
Identifying suspects by matching crime-scene DNA to distant relatives in public genealogy databases, then building the family tree inward.
DNA inherited only through the maternal line. Survives in degraded remains where nuclear DNA doesn't — common in cold case identifications.
Predicting physical traits — ancestry, eye color, hair color — from DNA alone, often used to generate suspect composites.
A fingerprint invisible to the naked eye, developed with powder, chemicals, or light sources.
The analysis of firearms, ammunition, and toolmarks — matching a bullet or casing to the weapon that fired it.
Microscopic particles expelled when a firearm is discharged. Presence suggests proximity to a shooting; absence proves little.
A chemical that fluoresces on contact with the iron in hemoglobin, revealing cleaned or invisible bloodstains. It points — it doesn't prove.
Reading the size, shape, and distribution of bloodstains to reconstruct events. Admissible but heavily contested science.
The medical examination of a body after death to establish cause and manner of death.
The specific injury or disease that ended a life — for example, asphyxiation or a gunshot wound.
The classification of how the cause arose: natural, accident, suicide, homicide, or undetermined.
Post-mortem muscle stiffening, beginning within hours and fully set around twelve — one of several clocks used to estimate time of death.
The settling of blood after death, staining the lowest parts of the body. Fixed lividity can show a body was moved.
Using insect evidence — species and life stage — to estimate how long a body has been where it was found.
Dental identification of remains, and the now-discredited practice of bite mark matching.
Chemistry that reads bones, teeth, and hair to reconstruct where a person lived and what they ate — a tool for identifying unknown remains.
Small transferred materials — fibers, hair, paint, glass, soil — that link people, places, and objects.
A known sample — handwriting, DNA, prints — collected from a person for comparison against evidence.
A database match that identifies a suspect with no prior connection to the investigation.
Someone investigators want to talk to. Not an accusation — a step below suspect.
A person investigators believe may have committed the crime, based on evidence.
An offender's method of committing crime — learned behavior that can evolve over time.
What an offender does beyond what's necessary to commit the crime — the psychological fingerprint that stays constant while an M.O. changes.
Deliberately altering a crime scene to mislead investigators — making a homicide look like a burglary gone wrong, for instance.
The study of the victim — routines, relationships, risk factors — to understand why they were targeted and by whom.
Systematic door-to-door interviews around a crime scene, hunting for witnesses and cameras.
'Be on the lookout' — an alert to law enforcement describing a person or vehicle of interest.
The public emergency alert for abducted children in credible, imminent danger — named for Amber Hagerman.
The National Missing and Unidentified Persons System — the public database that matches missing persons cases to unidentified remains.
The FBI's Violent Criminal Apprehension Program, linking violent crimes across jurisdictions by behavioral and physical details.
Inferring offender characteristics from crime scene behavior. A lead-generating tool, not evidence.
The investigative truism that solve rates drop sharply after the first two days — evidence degrades, memories fade, trails cool.
An unsolved case no longer under active investigation, kept open pending new leads or technology.
The court-ordered removal of buried remains for new examination.
Which agency owns a case — a frequent source of friction and, in serial cases, missed connections.
A multi-agency team assembled for one investigation, pooling jurisdiction and resources.
The public's channel into an investigation. High noise, occasionally the whole case.
A court order for data on every device inside an area during a time window — powerful and constitutionally contested.
A phone's contact with a tower, placing it in a general area — not a precise location, whatever TV says.
The legal threshold for arrests and warrants: enough facts for a reasonable person to believe a crime occurred.
The warnings required before custodial interrogation — silence and counsel. Unwarned statements risk suppression.
A grand jury's formal accusation, moving a case toward trial.
Citizens who review the prosecution's evidence in secret and decide whether charges proceed. They indict; they don't convict.
The first court appearance: charges read, plea entered, bail argued.
Resolving a case by agreement — a plea in exchange for reduced charges or sentence. How most criminal cases actually end.
A guilty plea in which the defendant maintains innocence while conceding the evidence would convict.
Accepting conviction without admitting guilt — often to limit exposure in a civil suit.
The criminal standard of proof — the highest in the legal system.
Evidence requiring an inference — fully legitimate, routinely conviction-grade, and routinely misunderstood.
Evidence that proves a fact without inference — an eyewitness, a confession, a recording.
An out-of-court statement offered for its truth. Generally inadmissible, with a long list of exceptions.
Evidence favorable to the defendant. Prosecutors must disclose it — that's Brady.
The state's failure to turn over exculpatory evidence — grounds for reversal.
The constitutional bar on retrying an acquitted defendant for the same offense.
The deadline for filing charges. Murder almost never has one.
Moving a trial when local publicity makes a fair jury impossible.
Jury selection — the questioning that surfaces bias before a juror is seated.
Isolating a jury from outside information during trial or deliberation.
A jury that cannot reach unanimity, ending in mistrial. The state may retry.
A trial terminated without verdict — for a hung jury, misconduct, or prejudicial error.
A not-guilty verdict. Not a declaration of innocence — a finding that proof fell short.
The formal clearing of a convicted person, often years later, by new evidence.
The post-conviction challenge to unlawful detention — the vehicle for many innocence claims.
A life sentence with no possibility of release — in practice, the alternative to capital punishment.
The claim that mental disease prevented understanding the act or its wrongfulness. Rarely raised, more rarely successful.
Whether a defendant can understand proceedings and assist counsel now — a different question from insanity at the time of the offense.
The formal transfer of a suspect between states or countries — and why some fugitives choose their refuge carefully.
An incarcerated witness trading testimony for benefit. A leading cause of wrongful convictions.
A conviction of the innocent — driven by misidentification, false confession, flawed forensics, and misconduct.
An innocent person's admission of guilt — produced by coercion, exhaustion, youth, or suggestion. It happens far more than intuition allows.
